rationale: The DSS metadata registry defines the data element and its DDMMYYYY format in the curated DEX attendance table, and the protocols set out the counting and reporting-period rules that depend on it.
evidence_quote: The date a given session took place, represented by DDMMYYYY.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'The date a given session took place.' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing said that this date drives the reporting-period counting rules or how it differs from the record-created dates.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, DEX Curated distributions
variable_description: The moment the record was first written to the Data Exchange, held for every versioned table in the extract rather than for one kind of record. It is an administrative timestamp, not a service fact: on the activity, organisation, outlet and client tables it sits with UPDATEDDATETIME, SYSSTARTTIME, SYSENDTIME, RECORDSEQNBR and CURRENTRECORD, which together make each table a versioned history. Use it to tell when a row entered the system, never to date the thing the row describes.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Client_Disability (DEX Curated) distribution
value_definition: A date and time. In the DEX curated tables it accompanies the system-time columns that bound each version of a row, so the creation stamp of a superseded version and of its replacement differ.
limitation: The timestamp cannot date the event the record is about. A session recorded three weeks after it happened, an activity created long after the programme began, or a client record migrated from another system will all carry a creation time that has no relation to the underlying date, which lives in CONDUCTEDDATE, STARTDATE or the client's own fields.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry shows CreatedDateTime in every curated DEX distribution alongside the system-versioning columns, but its definition is not published, so the timestamp reading rests on the custodian's wording and on the column's company rather than on a definition.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'The date and time that a given activity record was first created' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and appears on tables that are not activities, so a reader could not tell it is a general system-versioning column.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Client_Disability (DEX Curated) distribution, note on the disability code element
variable_description: Whether the row is the version in force or one the Data Exchange has since superseded, coded 1 for current and 0 for historical. Every versioned table in the extract carries it with RECORDSEQNBR, SYSSTARTTIME and SYSENDTIME, and DSS explains how it is set: "a service provider can delete a disability record, in which case CurrentRecord will be 0 and SysEndTime will be populated with the time that the service provider reported the disability was no longer current". Filtering on it is the difference between the state of the world now and everything ever reported.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Client_Disability (DEX Curated) distribution, note on the disability code element
value_definition: A two-state flag: 1 for the current version of a record, 0 for a superseded or deleted one, with SYSENDTIME populated when the value is 0.
limitation: A 0 does not mean the fact was wrong. It can mean the provider corrected an error, but equally that a circumstance changed or a record was tidied up, and the flag does not distinguish them. Filtering to current rows also does not guarantee one row per subject: DSS warns that a client may have no current disability records or several, so the flag controls currency, not cardinality.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry states the meaning of the two values and the condition that sets 0 in the curated DEX client disability table, and the same versioning columns appear on the activity, organisation, outlet, programme, service type and client tables in this extract.
evidence_quote: A service provider can delete a disability record, in which case CurrentRecord will be 0 and SysEndTime will be populated with the time that the service provider reported the disability was no longer current.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Flag that indicates whether a record is current (1) or historical (0)' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, so nothing told a reader what causes a row to become historical or that filtering to current rows still leaves duplicates.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Attendance (DEX Curated) distribution, note on the delivery organisation element
variable_description: The organisation that actually provided the service, which DSS distinguishes from the funded body: delivery organisations are "organisations delivering services directly to clients. These organisations may receive funding directly or through a Funding Recipient (Lead Organisation)." LEADORGID on the same row is the other half of that pair, so where the two differ the service was subcontracted through a consortium or delivery partnership. Join it to special_organisation for the organisation's ABN, and note that a delivery organisation may run several outlets, which OUTLETID identifies separately.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Attendance (DEX Curated) distribution, note on the delivery organisation element
value_definition: A system-generated whole number identifying an organisation record in the Data Exchange. It is not an ABN: ABN_HASH_TRUNC on the organisation table carries the hashed business number for the same organisation.
limitation: The identifier stands for an organisation as registered in the Data Exchange, not for a service or a site. One organisation can hold several identifiers where it registered separately for different programmes, and organisations that merge or re-register break a provider's history in two. Because the lead organisation is often also the delivery organisation, counting distinct values here does not count subcontracting arrangements.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the note distinguishing delivery organisations from lead organisations against these two fields in the curated DEX tables, and the protocols describe the delivery partnership and handshake arrangements that make the distinction matter.
evidence_quote: Organisations delivering services directly to clients. These organisations may receive funding directly or through a Funding Recipient (Lead Organisation)
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'A system-generated identifier for a unique service provider record in the Data Exchange, represented by a number' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, which conflates the delivering provider with the funded organisation beside it.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.1.8 and Table 7
variable_description: One disability, impairment or condition a client identified with, drawn from the AIHW groupings the protocols use: intellectual or learning, psychiatric, sensory or speech, physical or diverse, none, and not stated. Clients self-identify and "can identify with more than one group", which is why this sits in its own table with a row per report rather than as a column on the client record. DSS adds that the table "will contain records for any disability that has ever been reported", so CURRENTRECORD is what separates what a client reports now from what they once did.
description_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.1.8 and Table 7
value_definition: A short label held as an alphabetic code of seven to eleven characters in the registry's A(7)[AAAA] format. The protocols define each grouping by underlying condition, impairment, activity limitation and support need, giving examples: dyslexia under intellectual or learning, autism and depression under psychiatric, deafblindness under sensory or speech, and acquired brain injury under physical or diverse.
limitation: The grouping is not a diagnosis and not a severity measure. It is what a client chose to disclose to a service provider, so it undercounts conditions people do not volunteer, and it cannot be compared with a clinical or NDIS classification, which use different categories. 'None' and an absent row are also not the same: the first is a reported answer, the second is silence.
rationale: The protocols set out the AIHW groupings, define each with examples, list the six values in the priority client-level data table and state that clients may identify with more than one; the DSS metadata registry documents the resulting multi-row structure and its currency flag.
evidence_quote: When recording data about disability, impairments or conditions clients should self-identify, and can identify with more than one group, for example physical/diverse and intellectual/learning.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL wording and gave the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, so the page neither listed the groupings nor warned that a client can appear several times, including with superseded rows.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.3.1 and Table 10
variable_description: Which Department of Veterans' Affairs card the client holds, if any, across four responses: Gold Card, White Card, Orange Card or other, and no DVA entitlement. It is a Commonwealth Home Support Programme field, listed among items that "are required and will only present if the client is participating in the Commonwealth Home Support Programme activity", so a blank almost always means the client is in a different funded activity rather than that they hold no card. Within that programme it is the field that flags a veteran or war widow whose care may be funded through DVA rather than through aged care.
description_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.3.1 and Table 10
value_definition: One of four labels distinguishing the card types DVA issues, where a Gold Card covers treatment for all conditions, a White Card covers accepted conditions, and the Orange Card category absorbs other entitlements.
limitation: The card is not a service history and not proof of service. It records an entitlement status a client reported to a community care provider, so it will not match DVA's own records for people whose entitlement changed, and it says nothing about which conditions were accepted or what care DVA funded. Card status is also collected for the client, not for a partner who may be covered under the same entitlement.
rationale: The protocols name DVA card status as a Commonwealth Home Support Programme mandatory client field and list the four values in the programme's client-level data table, which is the list the registry already carries as this variable's valid values.
evidence_quote: DVA card status: a client's Department of Veterans' Affairs (DVA) card status is collected.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Department of Veteran's Affairs card status, represented by a code' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, so nothing told a reader the field exists for one programme and that blanks are structural.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 7.6 and Table 16
variable_description: The highest level of education or qualification a client had completed, on a nine-level scale running from pre-primary through certificate and diploma levels to postgraduate degree, with an 'other education' catch-all. The protocols say the item "lists qualifications and other educational attainments regardless of the particular field of study or the type of institution in which the study was undertaken", so it is attainment level only, with no field of study attached. It is optional partnership-approach data, unlike the demographic items in the priority client record, so coverage is patchy by organisation rather than by client.
description_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 7.6 and Table 16
value_definition: One of nine labels, ordered by level of attainment: pre-primary, primary, secondary, certificate, advanced diploma and diploma, bachelor degree, graduate diploma and graduate certificate, postgraduate degree, and other education.
limitation: The scale is not the ABS level of highest educational attainment classification and does not map cleanly onto it: 'secondary education' does not distinguish Year 10 from Year 12, and 'certificate level' merges Certificate I with Certificate IV. Nor is it a currency measure, because a qualification completed overseas or decades ago is recorded the same way as a recent Australian one. EMPLOYMENTSTATUSCODE beside it records study in progress, which this column does not.
rationale: The protocols describe what the item covers and list the nine levels in the partnership approach client-level data table, which is the list the registry already carries as this variable's valid values.
evidence_quote: Data is reported about highest educational achievement a person has attained. It lists qualifications and other educational attainments regardless of the particular field of study or the type of institution in which the study was undertaken.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL wording and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing said the scale is DEX's own rather than the ABS classification a reader would assume.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 7.2
variable_description: A flag for whether education was among the reasons a client sought assistance, from the domain the protocols word as "education and skills training: where the client is seeking to engage with education and skills training to improve their independence, participation and wellbeing". In this reference table that single published domain is carried across two columns, with TRAINING holding the skills training side, so both should be read together before concluding a client had no education-related need. EMPLOYMENT beside it is a separate domain, despite what the abbreviated column name suggests.
description_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 7.2
value_definition: A two-state flag, set when the education and skills training domain forms part of the combination that ASSISTANCENEEDEDKEY stands for. The domains are the eleven SCORE circumstance domains the protocols reuse as reasons for seeking assistance.
limitation: The flag is a presenting reason recorded by the provider, not an educational assessment, and it does not identify what the client wanted to study. Because the published domain is split across this column and TRAINING, either one alone undercounts the domain. Reporting is optional partnership-approach data, so a cleared flag mostly reflects an organisation that does not report reasons.
rationale: The protocols publish eleven reason categories including education and skills training, and this reference table carries one flag per category. The column name abbreviates education and employment, but its own description limits it to education, and a separate TRAINING column exists, so the split across two columns is read from the table rather than from the protocols.
evidence_quote: Education and skills training: where the client is seeking to engage with education and skills training to improve their independence, participation and wellbeing.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Seeking assistance related to education' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, which leaves a reader to guess from the column name that it covers employment, and gives no warning that the published domain is split across two columns.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 7.2 and 7.4
variable_description: Marks that lack of paid work was one of the things a client came for, or was referred on for. It is one flag among eleven on two small reference tables: on special_ref_assistance_needed a row is one combination of reasons for seeking assistance, reached from ASSISTANCENEEDEDKEY and PRIMARYASSISTANCENEEDEDKEY on the attendance record; on special_ref_referral_to a row is one combination of referral purposes, reached from REFERRALTOEXTERNALKEY and REFERRALTOINTERNALKEY. The protocols define the category as "to change the impact of a client's lack of employment on their independence, participation and wellbeing", and the same eleven categories drive the SCORE outcome domains, so a client's presenting reason and their rated outcome share one vocabulary.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 7.2 and 7.4
value_definition: A binary flag on a reference row rather than a value on a client record. A single key can set several flags at once, because a client may give more than one secondary reason and an organisation may refer for more than one purpose, so the reference table holds one row per observed combination rather than one row per category.
limitation: The flag says why the client presented, not whether they have a job. EMPLOYMENTSTATUSCODE on the client record is the employment measure, and the two often disagree: someone in insecure part-time work can present about employment, and an unemployed client can present about housing. Reasons are recorded at case level, so every attendance in a case repeats the same flag and counting attendances by reason counts sessions, not people.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols set out the eleven reason-for-seeking-assistance categories and the thirteen referral purposes by name and definition, and the reference tables in PLIDA carry one column per category with exactly those names.
evidence_quote: Employment: to change the impact of a client's lack of employment on their independence, participation and wellbeing.
supersedes_rationale: The entry showed the DIL fragment 'Seeking assistance related to employment' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation, so nothing said the column was a flag on a reference table or how it reached a client.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client: Employment status, Label' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution; DSS Data Exchange Protocols version 13, section 7.7
variable_description: What the client said they were doing for work when the record was created or last edited. DSS defines the element as "the employment status of a given client, whether employed or another role, represented by a label", and the label set mixes labour force states with unpaid roles: paid work full-time, paid work part-time, unpaid work including volunteering, unemployed and looking, not working and not looking, studying full-time, studying part-time, caring, and parenting. It is optional partnership-approach data, so it is present only for organisations that opted in and for clients who were asked.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client: Employment status, Label' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution; DSS Data Exchange Protocols version 13, section 7.7
value_definition: A short uppercase label rather than a numeric code, formatted A(6)[A(10)] in the DSS registry. The protocols state the categories are "adapted from the data collection definitions used by Disability Employment Services", not from the ABS labour force framework.
limitation: One label has to carry a person who does several things at once, and the protocols say so directly: a client's employment status can also include being a carer. A working parent, a studying carer and a part-time worker looking for more hours all resolve to a single value chosen by whoever entered the record. Because the categories come from Disability Employment Services rather than the ABS, the values cannot be aligned with a Labour Force Survey or Census employment status without a mapping that DSS does not publish.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the element definition and its format for the same column name in the curated Data Exchange client table, and the protocols publish the category list and its provenance.
evidence_quote: The employment status of a given client, whether employed or another role, represented by a label.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DSS wording as its description and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation, so nothing warned that a single label has to absorb caring, parenting and study.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols
variable_description: When a service activity stopped being available to deliver, not when anybody stopped receiving it. Paired with STARTDATE it bounds the funding arrangement's life, so an activity ending is a program or contract closing rather than a client exiting.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols
limitation: The date belongs to the activity, not to any client. An empty value means the activity was still available at extract, so it is censored rather than unknown. The domain is inferred from the DIL wording.
rationale: The DIL describes the field as the date a given activity is no longer available for service, on the Data Exchange activity table rather than a client table.
evidence_quote: The date that a given activity is no longer available for service.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DIL wording and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_domain: Data Exchange client exit reason label
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), section 7.16
variable_description: Why the client's involvement with a case ended, recorded on the attendance row that closed it. The protocols publish nine reasons: needs met, no longer requires assistance, service unable to assist, now requires a higher level of care, moved out of area, client terminated the service, client died, no longer eligible, and none of the above. Two of them turn on cause rather than outcome, and the protocols say so: needs met is for improvement "as a result of the reason they sought assistance and the service they received", while no longer requires assistance covers improvement "not necessarily because the service met their needs".
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), section 7.16
value_definition: One of nine published labels, unordered. The distinction between the two positive reasons is an attribution judgement made by the organisation, not a measured outcome.
limitation: Most cases carry no exit reason at all, because the field is optional partnership-approach data, so a missing value cannot be read as a case still open. The two positive categories are also not comparable across organisations: whether an improvement is credited to the service is a judgement, and an organisation with an incentive to show results has every reason to prefer needs met. Use the reason to describe how services end, not to measure whether they worked; the paired SCORE ratings are the outcome measure.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols publish the nine exit reasons with a definition of each and state the attribution distinction between the two positive categories in their own words.
evidence_quote: This may be used where a client's circumstances have improved to the point that they no longer require assistance, but not necessarily because the service met their needs.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the protocols' introductory sentence as its description and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without listing the reasons or flagging the attribution judgement inside them.

value_domain: Rural Financial Counselling Service external referral destination label
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), section 6.3.5 and the list of data values
variable_description: What kind of outside service a rural financial counselling client was sent on to. The protocols define it as an item "used to describe a client's referral to another service from the Rural Financial Counselling Service", and it is the only place in the Data Exchange that records a referral destination rather than a referral purpose. The twelve values are drawn from the world a farm business operates in: health professional, financial institution, legal aid or solicitor, accountant or financial adviser, real estate agent, agronomist, succession planner, social support group, training organisation, other government agency, asset agent, and other. It appears only for Rural Financial Counselling Service program activities and is empty on every other session.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), section 6.3.5 and the list of data values
value_definition: One of twelve published labels naming a type of destination, not a named organisation. The list is program specific and does not apply to, or align with, the general referral purpose categories used elsewhere in the Data Exchange.
limitation: A destination type is not evidence the client went. The Data Exchange records the referral as made and never records an arrival, so a count here measures counselling practice rather than client take-up. Because the field exists only for one program, it also cannot be used to compare referral behaviour between programs, and its absence on a session is not the absence of a referral: REFERRALTOEXTERNALKEY on the attendance record carries general external referrals with a purpose but no destination.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols define the item under Rural Financial Counselling Service mandatory fields and publish the twelve destination values in the list of data values.
evidence_quote: External Referral Destination: this item is used to describe a client's referral to another service from the Rural Financial Counselling Service.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the protocols' one-line definition and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, when the twelve destinations are published and the program restriction is what governs whether the column is usable.

value_domain: Data Exchange outcome domain flag (Family functioning)
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 7.2 and 7.4
variable_description: Marks that family functioning was one of the things a client came for, or was referred on for. The protocols define the category as "where the client is seeking to improve family functioning and change its impact on their independence, participation and wellbeing", which is about how a family works rather than about who is in it. It is one flag among eleven on the reasons-for-seeking-assistance reference table and one among thirteen on the referral-purpose reference table, both reached from key columns on the attendance record.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 7.2 and 7.4
value_definition: A binary flag on a reference row rather than a value on a client record. A single key can set several flags at once, so the reference table holds one row per observed combination of categories rather than one row per category.
limitation: Family functioning is not family safety. PERSONAL is a separate flag on the same row and carries personal and family safety, which is where domestic and family violence work sits, so reading this column as a violence indicator both overstates it and hides the safety caseload. It also says nothing about household structure: HOUSEHOLDCOMPOSITIONCODE on the client record is the only statement of who the client lives with.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols name and define family functioning as one of the eleven reason categories and one of the thirteen referral purposes, and they list personal and family safety separately.
evidence_quote: Family functioning: where the client is seeking to improve family functioning and change its impact on their independence, participation and wellbeing.
supersedes_rationale: The entry showed the DIL fragment 'Seeking assistance related to Family functioning' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, with no warning that a sibling column carries family safety.

value_domain: ABS Commonwealth Electoral Division code, 2022 boundaries
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard Edition 3, Non ABS Structures: Commonwealth Electoral Divisions
variable_description: The federal electorate an address falls in on the 2022 boundaries, assigned by the DSS address validation and geocoder rather than reported by anyone. The column appears on two tables and means two different things: on special_client it is the client's residential address, and on special_outlet it is the service outlet's address, where the DIL's own label still reads 'Client Address' and is wrong. ABS defines these divisions as "an ABS Mesh Block approximation of Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) federal electoral divisions", so the code is a statistical rendering of the electorate, not the AEC's legal boundary.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard Edition 3, Non ABS Structures: Commonwealth Electoral Divisions
value_definition: A three-digit code: one digit for state or territory and two digits for the division, numbered alphabetically within each state. The 2022 vintage is fixed, so the code reflects the AEC boundaries in force for that year and not any later redistribution.
limitation: An electorate changes under the feet of a person who never moves. The AEC redistributes divisions between elections, so this column cannot be compared with a division from another vintage, and a client appearing in a different electorate across two extracts has usually been re-coded rather than relocated. On the client table the underlying address is also unreliable for the people most likely to be studied: the protocols allow a homeless client to be recorded at the outlet's suburb and postcode, which puts them in the service's electorate.
rationale: The ABS publishes the definition, the coding structure and the AEC-approximation basis of Commonwealth Electoral Divisions in the ASGS non-ABS structures. The PLIDA registry shows the column on both the client and outlet tables with a geocoder-assigned description.
evidence_quote: Commonwealth Electoral Divisions are an ABS Mesh Block approximation of Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) federal electoral divisions.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL's 'Client Address: 2022 Federal Electorate Boundary Code' on both tables, which is wrong on the outlet table, and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_domain: Session fee in whole Australian dollars
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 6.3.1 and 6.3.2
variable_description: What the people attending a session were charged to be there. The protocols describe it as a session-level item that "allows organisations to report whether the participants of the session were charged a fee to attend the service and reflects the program activity policy regarding fee collection", captured as a dollar figure. It is a mandatory field only for Commonwealth Home Support Programme and Family Law Services activities, which are the two programs with a published fee policy, so it is empty across most of the Data Exchange.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 6.3.1 and 6.3.2
value_definition: A whole-dollar number recorded once for the session, appearing in the portal only where the selected program activity and service type make it applicable. The protocols call it a number field in whole dollars only.
limitation: The amount belongs to the session, not to a client, so it cannot be turned into a price per person without assuming the fee was split evenly among everyone who attended, which for family law mediation and group sessions it usually was not. A zero and a blank also read the same way to a reader but mean different things: zero is a session recorded as free, blank is a session where the question was never asked.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols define the item twice, once under Commonwealth Home Support Programme fields and once under Family Law Services fields, and give the units and the conditional presentation rule.
evidence_quote: Fees charged: this item is captured at the session level. It allows organisations to report whether the participants of the session were charged a fee to attend the service and reflects the program activity policy regarding fee collection. This item is captured as a dollar figure.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DIL wording and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying the amount is a session total or that the field only exists for two programs.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), section 4.5
variable_description: An indicator carried in from the geocoding of outlet addresses, not a property of the service. Its description in the data item list is not a description at all but the name of the source file, Dex1524outlet_geocoded_addr_a1, the same string that appears against ARID_HASH_TRUNC on the same table, so both columns came out of one address-matching run over Data Exchange outlet addresses for 2015 to 2024. On the evidence of that pairing and of the sibling columns ADDRESSSTATUSCODE, ARID_HASH_TRUNC, MB_ASGS_2021 and SA1_ASGS_2021, it marks how the outlet address resolved rather than anything a client or an organisation reported.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), section 4.5
value_definition: A small indicator, most likely binary, produced by the address matching process rather than reported by anyone. Neither the values nor their meanings are published.
limitation: Whatever the flag marks, it describes data processing and not service delivery, so it is never an analysis variable and a difference between outlets on this column is a difference in how their addresses were written down. Because the mapping is not published, a reader cannot tell whether a set flag means a good match or a problem one, and filtering on it risks dropping exactly the outlets whose addresses were hardest to place, which the protocols say include refuges and protected locations.
rationale: The data item list gives the same source file name for this column as for the outlet's address register identifier, which places it in the address geocoding output. No DSS or ABS document describing that output or its flags could be found, so the reading rests on the file name, the column name and the surrounding address columns.
supersedes_rationale: The entry showed the raw source file name 'Dex1524outlet_geocoded_addr_a1' as its description, guessed a yes-no domain from the variable name, and printed a boilerplate caveat as its limitation.

value_domain: ABS Standard for Sex, Gender, Variations of Sex Characteristics and Sexual Orientation Variables gender category
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols version 13, section 6.1.3; ABS Standard for Sex, Gender, Variations of Sex Characteristics and Sexual Orientation Variables
variable_description: The client's self-identified gender, and one of the four inputs to the linkage key that makes this dataset joinable at all. The protocols state that "a client's gender is recorded because it forms part of the SLK and is recorded based upon how the client self-identifies", and that the Data Exchange uses the ABS standard with five options: man or male, woman or female, non-binary, a different term, and prefer not to answer. This is a mandatory field, unlike most of the client attributes beside it.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols version 13, section 6.1.3; ABS Standard for Sex, Gender, Variations of Sex Characteristics and Sexual Orientation Variables
value_definition: A short label of up to eight characters in the DSS registry, drawn from the ABS gender standard rather than from a sex classification. ABS treats gender as "a social and cultural concept" about identity and experience, and consolidates free-text 'different term' responses with non-binary in published output.
limitation: Because gender feeds the statistical linkage key alongside name letters and date of birth, a client recorded as one gender at one organisation and another at a second generates two keys and appears in the data as two people. That makes the field a linkage risk as much as a demographic variable, and it makes a change of recorded gender over time indistinguishable from a data entry correction. The field is also not sex and cannot be used where a biological measure is wanted.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols state the collection rule, the ABS standard it follows and the five response options, and the same document sets out the linkage key algorithm that consumes the field.
evidence_quote: A client's gender is recorded because it forms part of the SLK and is recorded based upon how the client self-identifies.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried a garbled DIL sentence about male, female and 'other genders which are a combination of male and female' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, when the protocols publish the five options and their source.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026)
variable_description: A second identifier for the same organisation, carried in from the grants system rather than minted by the Data Exchange. It sits on both special_organisation and special_outlet beside ORGANISATIONID, which is the Data Exchange's own key, so the pair is what connects a service reporting performance data to the grant agreement that funds it. The Data Exchange draws activities from DSS grants systems, which SOURCESYSTEMCODE on the activity table records, and this is the organisation half of that provenance.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026)
value_definition: An opaque identifier issued by a DSS grants management system, not by the Data Exchange. Its format is not published and the value carries no readable structure.
limitation: Nothing in the data says what the grants system holds against this identifier, and a reader has no way to resolve it to a grant, a funding amount or an agreement period, because the grants data is not part of PLIDA. It is also not an entity identifier: two organisations under one grant, or one organisation with grants from several programs, need not have a one-to-one relationship with it. ABN_HASH_TRUNC on the organisation table remains the only key that matches a Data Exchange organisation to anything outside DSS.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols describe the grant-funded programs the Data Exchange reports on and the organisation and outlet structure the identifier sits in, but DSS publishes no documentation of GovGPS or of this identifier's format, so the reading is inferred from the column name, its placement beside the Data Exchange's own organisation key, and the presence of grants systems in SOURCESYSTEMCODE.
supersedes_rationale: The entry showed the DIL fragment 'Organisation GovGPS Organisation ID' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so the page said nothing beyond restating the variable name.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026)
variable_description: The grants system's identifier for a funded program activity, sitting on the activity table beside the Data Exchange's own ACTIVITYID and PROGRAMID. It is what ties an activity that clients attend to the funding line that pays for it, and it belongs to the same provenance chain as SOURCESYSTEMCODE on the same row, which records whether the activity came from a DSS grants system or from an external one. The activity is the level at which a program becomes something a client can attend from an outlet.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026)
value_definition: An opaque identifier issued by a DSS grants management system, not by the Data Exchange. Its format is not published and the value carries no readable structure.
limitation: The grants system is not in PLIDA, so the identifier cannot be resolved to a grant round, a funding amount or a contract term, and a change of value cannot be told apart from a re-let of the same service. It is also not a program classification: NAME and PROGRAMID on the same row carry the readable program and activity names, and this column will not group activities that a reader would consider the same program.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols describe program activities and the grant-funded programs behind them, and the activity table records its source system, but DSS publishes no documentation of GovGPS or of this identifier's format, so the reading is inferred from the column name and its placement beside the Data Exchange's own activity keys.
supersedes_rationale: The entry showed the DIL fragment 'GPS Program Activity ID' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so the page restated the variable name and nothing more.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client: Has a carer, Flag' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution; DSS Data Exchange Protocols version 13, section 6.3.1
variable_description: Whether somebody is caring for this client, which is the mirror image of ISCARER on the same row. DSS defines it as "whether a given client is the care recipient in a carer relationship, represented by a flag", and the protocols set it as a mandatory yes-or-no question for Commonwealth Home Support Programme activities, where it exists "to determine how many clients have care arrangements in place". Outside that programme it is rarely populated.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client: Has a carer, Flag' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution; DSS Data Exchange Protocols version 13, section 6.3.1
value_definition: A boolean flag, held as a single digit in the DSS registry. The carer concept behind it is the protocols' own: a person providing unpaid care and support to family or friends with a disability, mental illness, chronic or terminal condition, an alcohol or other drug issue, or who are frail aged.
limitation: The carer is not a person in this data. There is no carer identifier, no carer record and no link, so a care recipient cannot be paired with their carer even when both are Data Exchange clients and both have a row on special_client. Because the question is mandatory only for one programme, a blank almost always means the client was never asked rather than that nobody cares for them.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the element definition for the same column name in the curated client table, and the protocols state where the question is mandatory and what it is for.
evidence_quote: Whether a given client is the care recipient in a carer relationship, represented by a flag.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DSS wording as its description and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying that the carer is not represented anywhere in the data.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client: Homelessness status, Label' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution; DSS Data Exchange Protocols version 13, section 7.10
variable_description: Whether the client said they were homeless, at risk of homelessness, or neither. DSS defines the element as "the experience of unstable, inadequate or non-permanent housing identified by a given client, represented by a label", and the protocols set the three values as Yes, No and At Risk: a person is homeless if they have no suitable accommodation alternative and their current arrangement is in an inadequate dwelling, has no tenure or only short and non-extendable tenure, or does not allow control of and access to space for social relations. At risk covers major structural problems, constant threat of violence, crowding, improvised dwellings and marginal housing such as caravan parks.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client: Homelessness status, Label' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution; DSS Data Exchange Protocols version 13, section 7.10
value_definition: A short label of up to six characters in the DSS registry, holding one of three states rather than a yes-no flag. The three-part scale follows the ABS statistical definition of homelessness rather than a service eligibility test.
limitation: The value belongs to the client record, not to any session, so it is the answer as at the version of the client row you are reading. The row is versioned by SYSSTARTTIME, SYSENDTIME, RECORDSEQNBR and CURRENTRECORD, and joining the current version to an old session backdates a housing status that may have been recorded years later. The protocols also say the answer "should be based solely on what is reported by the client", so a service's own assessment never overrides it and a client who does not describe themselves as homeless is recorded as not homeless.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the element definition and format for the same column name in the curated client table, and the protocols publish the three values and the homelessness definition behind them.
evidence_quote: The experience of unstable, inadequate or non-permanent housing identified by a given client, represented by a label.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DSS wording as its description and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, when the protocols publish the three values, the definition and the self-report rule.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client: Household composition, Label' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution; DSS Data Exchange Protocols version 13, section 7.5
variable_description: Who the client lives with, in one of eight categories: living alone, sole parent with dependants, couple, couple with dependants, group of related adults, group of unrelated adults, homeless or no household, and not stated. The protocols state the categories are "adapted from the data collection definitions used by AIHW" and that the classification "is adapted to include data on whether the client is homeless". It is optional partnership-approach data, so absence is common and is not a household type.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client: Household composition, Label' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution; DSS Data Exchange Protocols version 13, section 7.5
value_definition: A label of up to ten characters in the DSS registry, formatted AAAAA[XAAAA]. Seven of the eight categories describe a living arrangement; the eighth records that there is no household to describe.
limitation: The other members of the household are not identified. There is no household key, no link between client records and no way to find a partner or a child who is also a Data Exchange client, so this column cannot be used to build households or to attribute a service to a family. The homeless category also makes the field two variables in one: a client coded Homeless/No household has an unknown living arrangement rather than a recorded one, so dropping that category from a distribution silently drops the most disadvantaged clients.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the element definition and format for the same column name in the curated client table, and the protocols publish the eight categories and state the AIHW basis and the homelessness adaptation.
evidence_quote: Household composition is classified into standard categories that are adapted from the data collection definitions used by AIHW. Household composition is adapted to include data on whether the client is homeless.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DSS wording 'Describes the client's living arrangements, represented by a label' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, when the protocols publish the eight categories.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 7.2 and 7.4
variable_description: Marks that housing was one of the things a client came for, or was referred on for. The protocols define the category as "where the client is seeking to improve their housing stability or address the impact of poor housing on their independence, participation and wellbeing", so it covers insecure and unsuitable housing as well as having none. It is one flag among eleven on the reasons-for-seeking-assistance reference table and one among thirteen on the referral-purpose reference table.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 7.2 and 7.4
value_definition: A binary flag on a reference row rather than a value on a client record. A single key can set several flags at once, so the reference table holds one row per observed combination of categories rather than one row per category.
limitation: This is a presenting reason, not a housing status. HOMELESSCODE on the client record carries the Yes, No or At Risk homelessness answer, and the two are only loosely related: a client in stable public housing can present about a repair dispute, and a homeless client often presents about money or safety instead. The Data Exchange also excludes the specialist homelessness services collection, so a DEX housing count is not a homelessness services count.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols name and define housing as one of the eleven reason categories and one of the thirteen referral purposes, and they define the homeless indicator separately at section 7.10.
evidence_quote: Housing: where the client is seeking to improve their housing stability or address the impact of poor housing on their independence, participation and wellbeing.
supersedes_rationale: The entry showed the DIL fragment 'Seeking assistance related to housing' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, inviting the reader to treat it as a homelessness flag.

value_domain: Self-reported gross income in whole Australian dollars
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), section 7.8.2
variable_description: How much the client said they earn, before tax, over whatever period INCOMEFREQUENCYCODE names. The protocols state that the field is "a numerical value for the estimated dollar amount of the client's gross income (earnings before tax)", that it "is based on what is reported by the client and no evidence of income is required", and that income frequency must be recorded for an amount to be recorded at all. It is optional partnership-approach data.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), section 7.8.2
value_definition: A whole-dollar number with no period attached to it. The web portal accepts the amount as a weekly, fortnightly, monthly or annual figure, so the number is uninterpretable on its own and has to be annualised against INCOMEFREQUENCYCODE before any two clients can be compared.
limitation: This is one person's estimate of their own income, not a measured or verified amount, and it is the client's income rather than the household's, so it cannot be used to place a client against a household income threshold or a poverty line. It is also a snapshot on a client record that changes only when someone edits it, so it is not a time series and cannot show an income change over a spell of service.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols set out the units, the gross basis, the self-report rule, the absence of verification and the dependency on income frequency for this exact field.
evidence_quote: Data is recorded as a numerical value for the estimated dollar amount of the client's gross income (earnings before tax). This is based on what is reported by the client and no evidence of income is required.
supersedes_rationale: The entry guessed a monetary domain from the variable name, described it as 'Descibes the amount of income that a given client receives', and gave a boilerplate limitation about inferred domains rather than warning that the figure is meaningless without the frequency.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), section 7.8.2
variable_description: The period the dollar figure in INCOMEAMOUNT refers to: weekly, fortnightly, monthly or annually. It exists because the Data Exchange lets clients answer in whatever period they think in, and the protocols make it compulsory whenever an amount is given, stating that "income frequency must be recorded in order to be able to record the approximate gross income". Without it the amount beside it cannot be read.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), section 7.8.2
value_definition: One of four period labels. The scale is not ordinal and carries no dollar information of its own; its only job is to supply the denominator for the amount on the same row.
limitation: The frequency is how the client chose to quote a figure, not how often they are actually paid, so it says nothing about pay cycle, casual work or the regularity of income. A client paid weekly who answers with an annual estimate is recorded as annual. It is also no help where the amount is missing: a frequency on its own conveys nothing.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols name the four frequencies in the list of data values and state the rule that binds this field to the income amount.
evidence_quote: Income frequency must be recorded in order to be able to record the approximate gross income.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DIL wording 'Describes the frequency of income that a given client receives' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, when the four values are published and the field's whole purpose is to make the amount readable.

value_domain: Data Exchange main source of income label
value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client: Main source of income, Code' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution; DSS Data Exchange Protocols version 13, section 7.8.1
variable_description: Where most of the client's money comes from, in one of six categories: nil income, employee salary or wages, self-employment from an unincorporated business, government payments, pensions and allowances, other income including superannuation and investments, and not stated. DSS defines it as "the main source of income for a given client, represented by a label", and the protocols state the categories are "based on the data collection definitions used by the AIHW". It is optional partnership-approach data reported alongside INCOMEAMOUNT and INCOMEFREQUENCYCODE.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client: Main source of income, Code' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution; DSS Data Exchange Protocols version 13, section 7.8.1
value_definition: A label of up to twelve characters in the DSS registry, formatted AAA[A(9)]. It names the largest single source only, not a composition, so it cannot be split or apportioned.
limitation: A main source hides mixed income. A client on a part-rate payment topping up part-time wages appears under one heading, so the column cannot measure reliance on income support or count people with any earned income. It is also the client's own account and is not reconciled with the payments data: someone coded to government payments here may have no DOMINO record, and someone coded to wages may be receiving a payment.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the element definition and format for the same column name in the curated client table, and the protocols publish the six categories and their AIHW basis.
evidence_quote: The main source of income for a given client, represented by a label.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DSS wording as its description and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, when the six categories are published and the main-source restriction is the field's central weakness.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), section 7.15
variable_description: Whether an interpreter was in the room for this session. The protocols define the field as reporting "whether an interpreter was present for the instance of service to assist with translation and facilitation", and are explicit that it counts either kind: "this could be an interpreter provided by the organisation or someone the client has brought along to help them". It is optional partnership-approach data recorded as yes or no at session level, so it varies within a client's history rather than sitting on the client record.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), section 7.15
value_definition: A yes or no flag on the session, one value per session rather than per attendee. It does not name a language and does not distinguish a professional interpreter from a family member acting as one.
limitation: Presence is not need. A session with no interpreter may be one where the client needed one and could not get one, which is the failure most worth finding, and this column cannot separate that case from a session where none was required. Because a family member counts, a high rate of interpreter presence is not evidence of professional interpreting being funded. MAINLANGUAGECODE on the client record is the closest thing to a need measure and it disagrees with this column often.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols define the field, state that it is session level and optional, and state that an interpreter brought by the client counts.
evidence_quote: This could be an interpreter provided by the organisation or someone the client has brought along to help them.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DIL wording and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying that an interpreter brought by the client counts or that absence does not mean no need.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client: Is a carer, Flag' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution; DSS Data Exchange Protocols version 13, section 7.12
variable_description: Whether the client says they care for somebody, which is the mirror image of HASCARER on the same row. DSS defines it as "whether a given client is a carer in a carer relationship, represented by a flag", and the protocols define a carer as "a person who provides unpaid care and support to family members and friends who have a disability, mental illness, chronic condition, terminal illness, an alcohol or other drug issue or who are frail aged". It is optional partnership-approach data recorded as yes or no.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client: Is a carer, Flag' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution; DSS Data Exchange Protocols version 13, section 7.12
value_definition: A boolean flag, held as a single digit in the DSS registry. The protocols state the field is "based on the client's reported caring situation", so it records identification rather than an assessment of caring hours or intensity.
limitation: Self-identification undercounts caring badly, because much of the care that meets the DSS definition is provided by people who describe themselves as a spouse, a parent or a daughter rather than a carer. The flag is also blank far more often than it is false, since it is optional, so treating a missing value as no inflates the non-carer group. Anyone counted here as a carer may separately appear with EMPLOYMENTSTATUSCODE of caring, and the two are collected under different rules.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the element definition and format for the same column name in the curated client table, and the protocols publish the carer definition and the self-report rule.
evidence_quote: A carer is defined as a person who provides unpaid care and support to family members and friends who have a disability, mental illness, chronic condition, terminal illness, an alcohol or other drug issue or who are frail aged.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DSS wording as its description and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, with nothing about the definition behind the flag or its known undercount.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 5.4 and 6.1.1
variable_description: Marks a client record built on a made-up name, and so a record that will not link. The protocols tell organisations that "where a client does not wish to disclose their real name, the organisation should indicate that a pseudonym is being used and record a pseudonym that ideally is used again if the client returns for other services". It matters far beyond privacy because the statistical linkage key is built from letters of the family and given name together with date of birth and gender, so a pseudonym changes the key.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 5.4 and 6.1.1
value_definition: A tick box in the web portal, carried into the data as a flag. It records that a pseudonym was used, not what the pseudonym was and not why.
limitation: The flag warns that a record is unlinkable but does nothing to repair it. A pseudonymous client's key is derived from a false name, so their service history will not join to their real records elsewhere in the Data Exchange or to any linked collection, and a client who used different pseudonyms at two organisations appears as two different people with no way to detect it. Pseudonym use is concentrated in refuge and family violence services, so the linkage loss is not random and falls on the clients most likely to be of interest.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols publish the pseudonym instruction, list the field as a tick box in the client data values, and set out the linkage key algorithm that consumes the client's name.
evidence_quote: Where a client does not wish to disclose their 'real' name, the organisation should indicate that a pseudonym is being used and record a pseudonym that ideally is used again if the client returns for other services.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Pseudonym used flag. Indicates clients who use pseudonym instead of their real name' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying that the flag marks a broken linkage key.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, LeadOrgId in the Attendance (DEX Curated) distribution
variable_description: Which organisation holds the money for the service this record belongs to. DSS describes lead organisations as "organisations that directly receive funding from grants" that "may also deliver the service, or allocate the funding to other Delivery Organisations", so the column is the funding recipient and DELIVERYORGID beside it is the provider. In a single-provider arrangement the two carry the same value; in a consortium they differ, and the difference between them is the only view the Data Exchange gives of subcontracting.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, LeadOrgId in the Attendance (DEX Curated) distribution
value_definition: A system-generated number of up to nineteen digits, following the same ID number domain as the other Data Exchange organisation and outlet keys. It is an internal key with no structure and no meaning outside the system.
limitation: Counting clients or sessions by lead organisation attributes a whole consortium's caseload to the head body, which for peak organisations and church-based networks can be tens of small services with nothing in common. The identifier also cannot be resolved to a named entity from the data alone: ABN_HASH_TRUNC on the organisation table is the only bridge to anything outside the Data Exchange, and it is a hash rather than a readable ABN.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the lead organisation and delivery organisation explanations against the same column names in the curated attendance table, and the protocols describe delivery partnership and consortium arrangements at section 4.6.
evidence_quote: Organisations that directly receive funding from grants. These organisations may also deliver the service, or allocate the funding to other Delivery Organisations.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DIL's parenthetical 'A lead org distributes funding to delivery orgs' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying that lead and delivery are equal in most rows and differ only under consortium arrangements.

value_domain: ABS Local Government Area code, 2016 boundaries
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard Edition 3, Non ABS Structures: Local Government Areas
variable_description: The council area an address falls in on the 2016 boundaries, assigned by the DSS address validation and geocoder. It appears on two tables with two meanings: on special_client it is the client's residential address and on special_outlet it is the outlet's, where the DIL's 'Client Address' label is a copy that was never corrected. ABS defines these areas as "an ABS Mesh Block approximation of gazetted local government boundaries as defined by each state and territory", and pairs on the same row with SA12016, SA22016, SA32016, SA42016 and STE2016, all cut from the same 2016 vintage.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard Edition 3, Non ABS Structures: Local Government Areas
value_definition: A five-digit code: one digit for state or territory and four for the area, always ending in zero. Parts of Australia that no incorporated council administers are carried as ordinary areas named Unincorporated followed by the state or territory. Separate non-spatial special purpose codes sit outside the legally designated areas as balancing items, for people coded to migratory, offshore and shipping mesh blocks, to no usual address, and to outside Australia.
limitation: The code is a statistical approximation and not the legal council boundary, so it must never be used to decide which council an address is rated by, which by-laws apply, or who is entitled to a council service. Parts of Australia have no incorporated council at all and still carry an ordinary code rather than a missing value, so an unincorporated area enters a distribution looking like a council.
rationale: The ABS publishes the definition, the five-digit coding structure and the special purpose codes for Local Government Areas in the ASGS non-ABS structures. The PLIDA registry shows the column on both the client and outlet tables with a geocoder-assigned description.
evidence_quote: Local Government Areas are an ABS Mesh Block approximation of gazetted local government boundaries as defined by each state and territory.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL's 'Client Address: 2016 Local Government Area Boundary Code' on both tables, which is wrong on the outlet table, and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_domain: ABS Local Government Area code, 2021 boundaries
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard Edition 3, Non ABS Structures: Local Government Areas
variable_description: The same address placed on the 2021 council boundaries, sitting next to the 2016 code rather than replacing it. Both editions are carried on special_client and special_outlet so that a record can be matched to whichever vintage a comparison dataset uses: the 2021 code aligns with the 2021 Census and with ASGS Edition 3 geography, the 2016 code with the 2016 Census. Where the two columns disagree for one row, the address did not move; the boundary did.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard Edition 3, Non ABS Structures: Local Government Areas
value_definition: A five-digit code: one digit for state or territory and four for the area, always ending in zero. There are 567 areas in the current release covering all of Australia, including unincorporated areas and nineteen non-spatial special purpose codes.
limitation: The 2021 and 2016 columns are not a before-and-after measure of anything about the client. Councils amalgamated and split between the editions and codes were reissued, so a series built by switching from one column to the other at 2021 shows a step change that is administrative. Choose one vintage for a whole analysis and match it to the vintage of whatever the geography is being joined to.
rationale: The ABS publishes the definition, coding structure and count of Local Government Areas in the ASGS non-ABS structures. That the two vintages sit side by side on the same PLIDA row, rather than one superseding the other, is read from the registry table structure rather than from a published statement.
evidence_quote: Local Government Areas are an ABS Mesh Block approximation of gazetted local government boundaries as defined by each state and territory.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL's 'Client Address: 2021 Local Government Area Boundary Code' on both tables and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing explained why two vintages of the same geography sit side by side.

value_domain: ABS Australian Standard Classification of Languages 2016, language code
value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client: Main language spoken at home, ASCL 2016 code' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution; ABS Australian Standard Classification of Languages, 2016
variable_description: The language the client says is mainly spoken in their home, coded to the ABS classification rather than written out. DSS names the element "Client: Main language spoken at home, ASCL 2016 code" and defines it as "the main language spoken at home by a given client, represented by a code". It is one of two cultural and linguistic diversity items collected as a priority requirement, the other being country of birth, and both are recorded as reported by the client.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client: Main language spoken at home, ASCL 2016 code' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution; ABS Australian Standard Classification of Languages, 2016
value_definition: A four-digit code from the Australian Standard Classification of Languages 2016, which covers 435 languages including 44 'not elsewhere classified' categories. The leading digit is the broad group and the first two digits the narrow group, so the code can be collapsed without a mapping table.
limitation: A language spoken at home is not a statement of English proficiency and not a statement of need for an interpreter. INTERPRETERPRESENT on the session record answers the second question and disagrees with this column often in both directions: a bilingual client who speaks another language at home may need no help, and a client who speaks English at home may attend with a parent who does not. The classification is fixed at the 2016 edition, which is the edition the 2021 Census also used, so the two line up; the ABS released a new edition in 2025, and language data coded on that edition will not join to this column without a correspondence.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry names the classification and edition in the element name for the same column in the curated client table and publishes the four-digit format. The ABS publishes the structure and scope of the 2016 classification.
evidence_quote: The main language spoken at home by a given client, represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DSS wording as its description and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without naming the classification the codes come from.

value_domain: Data Exchange outcome domain flag (Material wellbeing and basic necessities)
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 7.2 and 7.4
variable_description: Marks that an immediate shortage of money or basic goods was one of the things a client came for, or was referred on for. The protocols define the category as "to address the client's immediate lack of money and basic items needed for day-to-day living", which is the emergency relief end of the service system: food, bills, transport, a bed for the night. It is one flag among eleven on the reasons-for-seeking-assistance reference table and one among thirteen on the referral-purpose reference table.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 7.2 and 7.4
value_definition: A binary flag on a reference row rather than a value on a client record. A single key can set several flags at once, so the reference table holds one row per observed combination of categories rather than one row per category.
limitation: This is the immediate-shortage category, and MONEY on the same row is the separate financial resilience category. Adding the two together double counts a client flagged for both, and treating them as interchangeable merges emergency relief with financial counselling, which are different services with different clients and different lengths of engagement.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols define material wellbeing and basic necessities and financial resilience as two distinct categories in the same list of eleven, with different wording and different intent.
evidence_quote: Material wellbeing and basic necessities: to address the client's immediate lack of money and basic items needed for day-to-day living and to improve their independence, participation and wellbeing.
supersedes_rationale: The entry showed the DIL fragment 'Seeking assistance related to material wellbeing and basic necessities' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without distinguishing the column from the financial resilience flag beside it.

value_domain: ABS mesh block code, ASGS Edition 3 (2021)
value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard Edition 3, Main Structure: Mesh Blocks
variable_description: The service outlet's address placed in an ABS mesh block, which is the finest geography on the outlet record. ABS defines mesh blocks as "the smallest geographic areas defined by the ABS" that "form the building blocks for the larger regions of the Australian Statistical Geography Standard", and the SA1, SA2, SA4 and state columns beside it on special_outlet are all aggregations of this one code. It describes where a funded service is based, never where a client lives; the client geography sits on special_client.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard Edition 3, Main Structure: Mesh Blocks
value_definition: An eleven-digit code on the 2021 edition of the standard: one digit for state or territory and ten for the mesh block, as in 60106840000 for a Western Australian block. Mesh blocks are redefined at each Census, so a 2021 code has no counterpart in the 2016 columns on the same row.
limitation: A mesh block is a building block, not a place. ABS releases almost nothing at this level beyond dwelling and person counts, so the code is a key for aggregating up or for computing distance, not a unit anything can be described at, and mapping outlets by mesh block produces a picture nobody can read. It is also the outlet's location, so a distance from a client's mesh block measures how far the office is, which the protocols make clear is often not where the service happened.
rationale: The ABS publishes the mesh block definition, the eleven-digit code structure and the role of mesh blocks as the building block of the ASGS main structure. The column sits on the outlet table with the outlet's other geography.
evidence_quote: Mesh Blocks are the smallest geographic areas defined by the ABS and form the building blocks for the larger regions of the Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS).
supersedes_rationale: The entry guessed the domain from the variable name, showed the DIL fragment 'Mesh block coded to 2021 asgs' as its description, and gave a boilerplate limitation about inferred domains rather than saying that the geography belongs to the outlet.

value_domain: Data Exchange outcome domain flag (Mental health, wellbeing and self-care)
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 7.2 and 7.4
variable_description: Marks that mental health and self-care were among the things a client came for, or was referred on for. The DIL wording for this column, "Whether has mental and behavioural conditions", does not match what the Data Exchange collects: the protocols define the category as "where the client is seeking to change the impact of mental health issues and self-care issues on their independence, participation and wellbeing". It is one flag among eleven on the reasons-for-seeking-assistance reference table and one among thirteen on the referral-purpose reference table.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 7.2 and 7.4
value_definition: A binary flag on a reference row rather than a value on a client record. A single key can set several flags at once, so the reference table holds one row per observed combination of categories rather than one row per category.
limitation: The flag is not a diagnosis and not a health condition. It records why the client sought help, so a client managing a long-standing condition well and presenting about housing has this flag clear. Where a diagnosed condition is recorded at all, it is DISABILITYCODE on special_client_disability, which carries the psychiatric grouping described in the protocols. Reading this column as a prevalence measure counts service demand instead.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols name and define mental health, wellbeing and self-care as one of the eleven reason categories and one of the thirteen referral purposes. The disability groupings, including the psychiatric grouping, are defined separately at section 6.1.8.
evidence_quote: Mental health, wellbeing and self-care: where the client is seeking to change the impact of mental health issues and self-care issues on their independence, participation and wellbeing.
supersedes_rationale: The entry showed the DIL wording 'Whether has mental and behavioural conditions', which misdescribes the field as a health condition, and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_domain: Data Exchange outcome domain flag (Financial resilience)
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 7.2 and 7.4
variable_description: Marks that financial resilience was one of the things a client came for, or was referred on for. The protocols define the category as "where the client is seeking to improve financial resilience and change its impact to improve the client's independence, participation and wellbeing", which is about managing money and debt rather than about how much of it there is. It is one flag among eleven on the reasons-for-seeking-assistance reference table and one among thirteen on the referral-purpose reference table.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols, version 13 (effective 1 March 2026), sections 7.2 and 7.4
value_definition: A binary flag on a reference row rather than a value on a client record. A single key can set several flags at once, so the reference table holds one row per observed combination of categories rather than one row per category.
limitation: The flag carries nothing about the level of income.
