Only one setting is recorded per session, so a service that began on the phone and finished in person appears as whichever the organisation judged dominant. It also describes the delivery channel, not the client's whereabouts: a telephone session says nothing about where the client was sitting.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the data element with its definition and full permissible value list, and the protocols give a plain description of each setting category and record the addition of the Video category.
evidence_quote: The category of physical location or delivery method for a given session, represented by a label.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried source-defined values with the boilerplate 'The valid_values field contains the source-defined values' as its definition and 'The source defines the value domain' as its limitation, and never contrasted the setting with the outlet.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Session: Service type, Code', Aristotle item 1289
variable_description: The kind of help delivered, defined by DSS as "the main focus of service delivery at a given session, represented by a code". The codes begin at 1 for intake or assessment and 2 for information, advice and referral, and continue through education and skills training, child and youth focused groups, counselling and dispute resolution. Which of them an organisation may use depends on the program activity, because the Data Exchange portal offers only the service types attached to the activity being reported, and special_service_type is the lookup that gives each code its name.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Session: Service type, Code', Aristotle item 1289
value_definition: A number of up to three digits from a single registry-wide list dating from 20 June 2014. The list is long, and the subset available for any one program activity is published in that program's guidance rather than in the protocols.
limitation: Only one service type is recorded per session, so the column understates what a session contained: counselling that also arranged a referral is recorded as counselling alone, on the protocols' rule that the type taking most of the time or achieving the outcome wins. The codes are shared across programs but the menus are not, so a national count by service type mixes activities that use one code for quite different work.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the session service type data element with its definition, three-digit format and coded values. The protocols set the rule for choosing among several types and state that the portal restricts the list by program activity.
evidence_quote: The main focus of service delivery at a given session, represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified' with the generic no-value-list sentence used for both the definition and the limitation, even though the registry publishes a coded list.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Session: Conducted date, DDMMYYYY', Aristotle item 890
variable_description: The date of the session a SCORE assessment relates to, defined by DSS as "the date a given session took place, represented by DDMMYYYY". On the assessment tables it is the anchor for ordering initial and subsequent ratings, and it is the date that decides which reporting period the assessment counts against, unlike SESSIONCREATEDDATE and ASSESSMENTCREATEDDATE, which record when the record was keyed in. CONDUCTEDDATE on special_attendance carries the same fact for attendance rows.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Session: Conducted date, DDMMYYYY', Aristotle item 890
value_definition: A calendar date at day resolution, registered in DDMMYYYY form with no time component. The protocols require session dates to be entered as dd/mm/yyyy.
limitation: The date belongs to the session, not to the assessment, so several ratings, several domains and several clients share one value and it cannot order two assessments made on the same day. DSS notes that since 18 August 2018 the service phase label is no longer the primary means of ordering assessments either. It also dates the rating, never the change in circumstances being rated.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the session conducted date element with its definition and DDMMYYYY format, and the curated client assessment distribution shows how the assessment record hangs off the session.
evidence_quote: The date a given session took place, represented by DDMMYYYY.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified' and the generic no-value-list sentence stood as both value definition and limitation, so nothing warned that the date belongs to the session rather than the assessment.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client outcome assessment: Created date, DDMMYYYY', Aristotle item 1672, the created-date element registered for this table
variable_description: When the session record was first entered into the Data Exchange, as against SESSIONCONDUCTEDDATE, which is when the session happened. The gap between the two is reporting lag: organisations may enter data at any point in a six-month reporting period and for 30 days after it closes, so a session held in January can be created in August. Use it to judge how current the data was and to spot bulk loads, never to date the service.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Client outcome assessment: Created date, DDMMYYYY', Aristotle item 1672, the created-date element registered for this table
value_definition: A date and time stamped by the system when the record was written. The sibling element on this table, ASSESSMENTCREATEDDATE, is registered as the date a record "was entered into a system" in DDMMYYYY form, so expect day resolution at best from the date part.
limitation: It dates the record, not the event, and it is a system value rather than a service fact: a bulk upload creates thousands of session records within one second, and a system migration can restamp records that describe much older sessions. A long gap from the conducted date is a sign of late reporting, not of a long service.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the created-date concept for this curated table and defines it as the date a record was entered into a system, which is the domain this column carries. The protocols supply the reporting period and close-off rules that explain how large the lag can be.
evidence_quote: The date a given client outcome assessment was entered into a system, represented by DDMMYYYY.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified' and the generic no-value-list sentence appeared as both the definition and the limitation, leaving the crucial contrast with the conducted date unsaid.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Data Exchange: Session identifier, ID number', Aristotle item 1775
variable_description: The key of a single instance of service, which DSS defines as "a system-generated identifier for a unique session record in the Data Exchange, represented by a number". The protocols define a session as an individual episode of service stored within a case, and this is the column that holds the session tables together: special_session has one row per session, special_attendance one row per person present, and the assessment tables hang their SCOREs off the same value. Organisations uploading in bulk supply their own session identifier, and the Data Exchange generates one only when the portal field is left blank.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 'Data Exchange: Session identifier, ID number', Aristotle item 1775
value_definition: A number of up to 19 digits, registered with the format N[N(18)]. It is unique within the case rather than globally meaningful, and the identifier the provider supplied is limited to 50 characters before the Data Exchange converts it.
limitation: A session is a reporting construct, not a unit of effort: a two-hour group workshop and a five-minute phone call are each one session, so session counts are not workload and ASSISTANCEMINUTES is the column for that. The curated attendance table also writes aggregate rows for unidentified clients using the negative of the session identifier as the attendance key, so naive counts of attendance identifiers within a session can be thrown out by those rows.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the session identifier data element with its definition and format, and the curated attendance distribution documents the negative-identifier convention used for unidentified client attendance. The protocols define the session concept and the identifier's business rules.
evidence_quote: A system-generated identifier for a unique session record in the Data Exchange, represented by a number.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, and the custodian's description said nothing about how sessions relate to cases, attendances or assessments.

rationale: The PLIDA description supplies two real values (FOFMS, EXTNL) and the field is a short uppercase mnemonic identifying the DSS system that supplied the activity record. I searched the DEX Protocols v13, the Bulk File Upload Technical Specification (Nov 2025) and the Web Services Technical Specification v1.11 and none of them contains a source-system code list; it is an internal DSS warehouse field, so the two documented values are the whole defensible domain.
supersedes_rationale: The earlier reviewer noted the two examples are not a complete codeframe, which is true, but two real published values are enough for a coarse inferred domain.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols
variable_description: When a service activity became available to deliver, not when anybody received it. The Data Exchange models a funded service as an activity with an availability window, and clients attach to it through separate session records, so this is a property of the funding arrangement. Using it as a service start date for a client attributes the whole activity's lifetime to everyone who touched it.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols
limitation: The date belongs to the activity, not to any client, and says nothing about when service was actually delivered. The domain is inferred from the DIL wording; the Data Exchange publishes its protocols but not this field's definition.
rationale: The DIL describes the field as the date a given activity is available for service, on the Data Exchange activity table rather than a client table.
evidence_quote: The date that a given activity is available for service.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DIL wording and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying that the date belongs to the activity rather than a client.

value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Australia and State/Territory
variable_description: The state or territory of the outlet's address as ABS coded it under ASGS Edition 3, and the top of the hierarchy the SA1, SA2 and SA4 columns beside it belong to. ABS records that "in general, the total area of each State and Territory, including their offshore islands, is used for statistical purposes as a separate geographic area in the ASGS". OUTLETSTATE on the same row is the state the organisation typed in, so the two can disagree wherever the entered address was wrong or out of date, and this one follows the geocoded address.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Australia and State/Territory
value_definition: A one-digit code: 1 New South Wales, 2 Victoria, 3 Queensland, 4 South Australia, 5 Western Australia, 6 Tasmania, 7 Northern Territory, 8 Australian Capital Territory and 9 Other Territories. It is also the leading digit of the SA1, SA2 and SA4 codes on the same row, so the three are internally consistent by construction.
limitation: Code 9 is a bundle rather than a place: Jervis Bay Territory and the Christmas Island, Cocos (Keeling) Islands and Norfolk Island territories are one category and cannot be separated. The value also describes the premises, so a national help line run from one office puts all of its sessions in a single jurisdiction, which is a poor basis for comparing service levels between states.
rationale: ABS publishes the state and territory coding structure for ASGS Edition 3, with the one-digit codes and the treatment of Other Territories. The custodian's own description of the column as 'State (number)' confirms it is the numeric ABS code rather than an abbreviation.
evidence_quote: In general, the total area of each State and Territory, including their offshore islands, is used for statistical purposes as a separate geographic area in the ASGS.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the state codeframe with the boilerplate 'The valid_values field contains the source-defined values' as its definition and 'The source defines the value domain' as its limitation, and never distinguished it from the organisation-entered OUTLETSTATE.

value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS): Volume 1 - Main Structure and Greater Capital City Statistical Areas, July 2016
variable_description: The state or territory the DSS geocoder derived from the address on the record, on the 2016 ASGS boundaries: the client's residence on special_client and the outlet's premises on special_outlet. Of the whole boundary code family this is the one that almost never changes between vintages, which makes it the safest fallback when a finer code failed to resolve. The curated Data Exchange client table carries the 2011, 2016 and 2021 state codes side by side.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS): Volume 1 - Main Structure and Greater Capital City Statistical Areas, July 2016
value_definition: A one-digit code from 1 to 9 on the ASGS July 2016 edition, with 9 covering the Other Territories. It is the leading digit of the SA1, SA2, SA3 and SA4 boundary codes on the same row, so it can be derived from any of them.
limitation: State boundaries barely move, so a row where the 2016 and 2021 state codes differ is evidence of an address edit or a geocoding change rather than of a boundary revision, and treating the pair as a migration signal will produce false moves. For a client, the state is the state of the address recorded, which the protocols allow to be the outlet's address where the client is homeless or at risk.
rationale: ABS published the state and territory coding for the July 2016 ASGS edition the column names, and DSS's curated client distribution lists the 2011, 2016 and 2021 state boundary columns as one geocoded family.
evidence_quote: Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS): Volume 1 - Main Structure and Greater Capital City Statistical Areas, July 2016
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the ABS state codeframe with the boilerplate definition and the generic 'The source defines the value domain' limitation, saying nothing about the vintage pairing or the address substitution rules.

value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Australia and State/Territory
variable_description: The state or territory of the address on ASGS Edition 3 boundaries, assigned by the DSS geocoder to the client record and to the outlet record. It is the coarsest of the 2021 boundary codes and the one most Data Exchange program reporting is broken down by, because activities are commissioned jurisdiction by jurisdiction. On special_outlet it should agree with STATE_ASGS_2021, which ABS derived independently through the address register match.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Australia and State/Territory
value_definition: A one-digit code from 1 to 9 under ASGS Edition 3, July 2021 to June 2026, where 9 is Other Territories. Australia itself is coded AUS in Edition 3, replacing the numeric 036 used in the 2016 edition.
limitation: It does not identify who funds or administers the service. DSS is a Commonwealth department, several Data Exchange program values belong to state agencies, and a client's state and the funding jurisdiction are separate questions. Nor is it a reliable statement of usual residence: a client can move between service episodes without the address on their record being updated.
rationale: ABS publishes the state and territory codes and the Other Territories treatment for the edition named in the column. DSS's curated client distribution lists this column with the rest of the 2021 boundary set produced by its geocoder.
evidence_quote: States and Territories are identified by unique one-digit codes
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the ABS state codeframe with the boilerplate definition and the generic limitation, and gave no indication that the same fact appears twice on special_outlet from two different geocoding paths.

value_source: ABS, Person Level Integrated Data Asset (PLIDA)
variable_description: The person key that runs through the Data Exchange tables: one client carries the same value across special_client, special_attendance, special_client_assessment, special_client_disability and special_community_assessment, which is what turns scattered session rows into a service history. It is the DSS client identifier in anonymised form, not a PLIDA-wide person number: ABS links datasets through a "Person Linkage Spine" held "separate from the main body of data", so joining a Data Exchange client to their Medicare, tax or payment records means going out through the agency spine file to the spine identifier and back in through another agency's identifier.
description_source: ABS, Person Level Integrated Data Asset (PLIDA)
value_definition: An opaque identifier with no internal structure and no decodable content. It is stable within the DSS extract and meaningless outside it, so it can be compared for equality and nothing else.
limitation: It identifies a client record, not a person. The Data Exchange creates client records at the delivery organisation level, so someone who registers with two providers under different details can hold two identifiers until the statistical linkage key brings them together. Linkage to the PLIDA spine also fails for a share of records, and an unlinked client is missing from the other datasets rather than absent from them.
rationale: ABS documents the Person Linkage Spine as the mechanism by which agency datasets are linked, held separately from the data itself, which is why each agency's records carry their own anonymised person identifier rather than a shared one. The curated Data Exchange client distribution shows client records are held against a delivery organisation, which is what makes duplicate client records possible.
evidence_quote: The Person Linkage Spine allows us to link datasets through a spine of key information, separate from the main body of data.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was guessed from the variable name as an opaque identifier, and the limitation only restated that the domain was inferred and open, which told a reader nothing about how to join the column or where linkage fails.

value_source: Microsoft, SQL Server temporal tables documentation, which defines the SysStartTime and SysEndTime period columns this pair follows
variable_description: The moment this version of the row stopped being the current one. The seven reference tables that carry it — activity, client, client disability, organisation, outlet, program and service type — are delivered as full row histories rather than snapshots, and SYSSTARTTIME and SYSENDTIME bound the window in which each version was live. The current version carries the maximum value the type allows rather than a null, so the filter for a snapshot is SYSENDTIME at its maximum, or equivalently CURRENTRECORD set to 1.
description_source: Microsoft, SQL Server temporal tables documentation, which defines the SysStartTime and SysEndTime period columns this pair follows
value_definition: A datetime in UTC closing a version's period. Following the system-versioned temporal table convention the columns are named for, the open row is given 9999-12-31 23:59:59.9999999 rather than a null, so comparisons against a null will silently drop the current record.
limitation: It records when the database row was superseded, not when the thing it describes ended: an outlet that closed in March but was edited in September ends its version in September. ENDDATE on special_activity is the service fact — the date an activity is no longer available for service — while this column is only the record's lifetime in the system.
rationale: The column names, the accompanying CURRENTRECORD flag and RECORDSEQNBR counter, and the presence of SysStartTime and SysEndTime in DSS's own curated Data Exchange client table all match the system-versioned temporal table pattern, whose period column semantics and open-row sentinel value are published by Microsoft. The specific values DSS stores are not published, hence medium confidence.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both the definition and the limitation, so nothing told a reader that failing to filter this column multiplies every entity by its version count.

value_source: Microsoft, SQL Server temporal tables documentation, which defines the SysStartTime and SysEndTime period columns this pair follows
variable_description: The moment this version of the row became current. Reading any of the seven reference tables without filtering on it counts one outlet, client or activity several times over, because the product ships every version of every reference record rather than a snapshot. Paired with SYSENDTIME it gives the window in which the row was live, and RECORDSEQNBR numbers the same versions in the same order. A record that has never been edited has one version, whose start time is when it was first written.
description_source: Microsoft, SQL Server temporal tables documentation, which defines the SysStartTime and SysEndTime period columns this pair follows
value_definition: A datetime in UTC opening the period during which this version was current. Under the system-versioned convention the columns are named for, one version's end time equals the next version's start time, so the periods abut exactly and leave no gaps in an entity's history.
limitation: It is a database write time, so it dates the data entry rather than the event: a client record created in 2019 that describes services from 2016 carries a 2019 start time. It also cannot be read across tables as a measure of when anything happened, because a bulk load stamps thousands of unrelated rows with a single time.
rationale: The pairing with SYSENDTIME, the CURRENTRECORD flag and RECORDSEQNBR, together with DSS listing SysStartTime and SysEndTime in its own curated Data Exchange client table, identify these as system-versioned period columns, whose semantics Microsoft publishes. DSS does not publish the stored values, hence medium confidence.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified', the generic no-value-list sentence was printed as both definition and limitation, and the description was the custodian's five words, 'Record start date and time'.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols, Version 11, March 2024, sections 3.4 and 10.3
variable_description: The calendar date a Data Exchange calendar-table row stands for. Every other column on the row is derived from it: THEDAY, THEDAYNAME, THEDAYOFWEEK, THEWEEK, THEISOWEEK, THEMONTH, THEQUARTER, THEYEAR and THEFINANCIALYEAR, with THEREPORTINGPERIOD and REPORTINGPERIODENDTIME placing it in one of the two six-monthly reporting periods. It exists so a session's conducted date can be joined to consistent period labels rather than each analyst deriving their own, which matters because the protocols count a session against a reporting period by its date.
description_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols, Version 11, March 2024, sections 3.4 and 10.3
value_definition: A calendar date at day resolution and the primary key of special_ref_calendar, with one row for every day the table spans, weekends and public holidays included.
limitation: The table describes the calendar, not the data: a date is present whether or not any session occurred on it, so counting rows here measures the span of the calendar and never activity. Joining to it cannot fill gaps either — a day with no sessions simply produces no match on the other side of the join.
rationale: The protocols set the counting rule that a session belongs to the reporting period its date falls in, and define the two six-monthly periods, which is what this date dimension exists to implement. The registry's own column list for special_ref_calendar shows the derived date parts that hang off this key.
evidence_quote: A session is counted against a reporting period if the date of the session fell within the reporting period and at least one client is attached.
supersedes_rationale: The domain was 'not specified', the generic no-value-list sentence stood as both definition and limitation, and the description was the custodian's catch-all 'Calendar related data fields', shared with fourteen other columns in the table.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions
variable_description: The day-of-month number for one row of the Data Exchange calendar, which holds one row per date rather than one row per client or service. The calendar exists because everything in the Data Exchange is counted by the date of a session, so THEDATE on the same row is the date itself and THEDAY, THEMONTH and THEYEAR are its parts, pre-computed for joining and grouping. Nothing on this row belongs to a person, an outlet or an organisation.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions
value_definition: A whole number from 1 to 31, the day component of the Gregorian date held in THEDATE on the same row. It is a calendar attribute, not a duration and not a count.
limitation: The number cannot order or identify a date on its own, because the 3rd of one month and the 3rd of the next share a value, so grouping by it pools every month together. It also tells you nothing about service delivery until the calendar table is joined to a session or assessment table on the date.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols fix why a date matters in this collection: sessions, cases and clients are all counted against a reporting period by session date. The column-level reading is inferred from the sibling columns in special_ref_calendar, which are the standard parts of a warehouse date dimension (THEDATE, THEDAYNAME, THEDAYOFWEEK, THEDAYOFYEAR, THEWEEK, THEISOWEEK, THEMONTH, THEMONTHNAME, THEQUARTER, THEYEAR), and no DSS document defines the warehouse column itself.
evidence_quote: A session is counted against a reporting period if the date of the session fell within the reporting period and at least one client is attached.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's blanket wording, 'Calendar related data fields', for every column in the table, and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both its value definition and its limitation.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions
variable_description: The name of the weekday for one row of the Data Exchange calendar, spelled out rather than numbered. THEDAYOFWEEK beside it carries the same fact as an index, so the two never disagree and only one of them is needed. Joined to the session tables it answers whether a funded activity was delivered on weekends, which differs sharply between family services and emergency relief.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions
value_definition: A weekday label in English, one of the seven names from Monday to Sunday, derived from the date in THEDATE on the same row.
limitation: A weekday label says nothing about whether an outlet was open, whether the day was a public holiday, or whether staff worked it, because the Data Exchange holds no opening hours or holiday calendar. Session dates are also often entered in bulk well after the event, so an unlikely-looking day pattern can be a data-entry habit rather than a delivery pattern.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols establish that the session date drives all counting, which is what the calendar table serves. The column meaning is inferred from the name and from THEDAYOFWEEK sitting beside it as the numeric form; no DSS document defines the warehouse column.
evidence_quote: A session is counted against a reporting period if the date of the session fell within the reporting period and at least one client is attached.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the table-wide description 'Calendar related data fields' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation.

rationale: The field sits in the DEX calendar dimension table special_ref_calendar alongside THEDAY, THEDAYNAME, THEDAYOFYEAR, THEWEEK, THEISOWEEK, THEMONTH and THEMONTHNAME; with a separate THEDAYNAME holding the weekday label, THEDAYOFWEEK is the numeric weekday index taking 1 to 7. The numbering convention (Sunday-first as in SQL Server DATEPART, versus Monday-first as in ISO 8601) is not published, so only the range is claimed.
supersedes_rationale: The earlier determination treated the vague description ('Calendar related data fields') as fatal, but the variable name and its sibling columns fix the domain to a 1-7 weekday index.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions
variable_description: The position of the date within its calendar year, counting 1 January as day one. On the Data Exchange calendar it is the attribute that lets service volumes be lined up across years without month boundaries getting in the way, which is how seasonal demand for emergency relief or financial counselling is usually looked at. It is a property of the date alone and repeats identically for every year in the table.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions
value_definition: A whole number from 1 to 365, or to 366 in a leap year, counted from 1 January of the year in THEYEAR on the same row.
limitation: The number does not map to the same calendar date in every year: after February a leap year shifts everything by one, so aligning years on this column misaligns the dates by a day. It also cuts across the Data Exchange reporting cycle, which runs in six-month halves from 1 July, so a day-of-year series cannot be tied back to a reporting period without THEREPORTINGPERIOD.
rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols establish the date-driven counting the calendar table supports. The 1 to 366 domain is inferred from the column name and from the sibling calendar columns; no DSS document defines the warehouse column.
evidence_quote: A session is counted against a reporting period if the date of the session fell within the reporting period and at least one client is attached.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the table-wide description 'Calendar related data fields' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_domain: Australian financial year, 1 July to 30 June
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Quick Start Guide (April 2020), 'Start entering data'
variable_description: The July-to-June year the date falls in, which is the year Data Exchange funding agreements and performance reporting run on. The Quick Start Guide sets the cycle out as two halves: "There are two reporting periods per year which run from 1 July to 31 December and 1 January to 30 June, with a 30 day close off period to allow you to finalise your data." This column names the pair of halves taken together, while THEREPORTINGPERIOD on the same row names which half.

limitation: It is not the calendar year in THEYEAR, and the two disagree for every date between January and June, so mixing them splits a single year of activity across two labels. It also says nothing about whether the reporting period was still open when a record was entered, because organisations have a further 30 days after each half closes.
rationale: The Quick Start Guide states the two reporting periods, which together define the 1 July to 30 June year this column labels. The exact text format of the label is not published, so only the boundaries are claimed.
evidence_quote: There are two reporting periods per year which run from 1 July to 31 December and 1 January to 30 June, with a 30 day close off period to allow you to finalise your data.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the table-wide description 'Calendar related data fields', which did not distinguish a financial year from a calendar year, and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

THELASTOFYEAR beside it does the same job at the other end of the year.

evidence_quote: A session is counted against a reporting period if the date of the session fell within the reporting period and at least one client is attached.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the table-wide description 'Calendar related data fields' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions
variable_description: The ISO 8601 week that this calendar row's date falls in, kept separately from THEWEEK because the two count weeks by different rules. Under ISO 8601 a week runs Monday to Sunday and week 1 is the week containing the first Thursday of the year, so the ISO week is the one to use when weekly service counts have to line up with any external weekly series. Joined to the session tables it gives a weekly view of delivery inside a six-month reporting period.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 3.4 counting rules for clients, cases and sessions

value_domain: count of unidentified attendees at a session
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), sections 2.6 and 5.2.2, and Table 9 priority requirements session level data
variable_description: How many people attended a session without a client record being created for them. The Protocols define the item as "the aggregate number of unidentified clients who attended a session" and say it "should be limited to large groups where the collection of client level information is not feasible", which in practice means public events, information sessions and community outreach. These attendances are the only trace those people leave: they have no client row, no demographics and no person identifier, so nothing about them can be linked to the PLIDA spine.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), sections 2.6 and 5.2.2, and Table 9 priority requirements session level data
value_definition: A count of people on the session record, defaulting to zero, entered as a number up to 999, and constrained so that it cannot exceed the case-level figure carried in UNIDENTIFIEDCLIENTCASEMAX.
limitation: The number counts attendances at one session, not people: someone who comes to three sessions is counted three times, and the file gives no way to tell repeat attendance from new attendance. It also carries no age, sex, Indigenous status or cultural and linguistic background, so an event's audience cannot be described at all. Any person-level analysis of the Data Exchange silently drops these people while service-level counts keep them, which is the usual source of a mismatch between the two.
rationale: The Protocols define the session-level item, give its purpose, and specify the field as a number with a default of zero and a maximum of 999 that cannot exceed the case-level value.
evidence_quote: Unidentified client attendance: the aggregate number of unidentified clients who attended a session. This should be limited to large groups where the collection of client level information is not feasible.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'The number of unidentified clients for the session', which did not explain who these people are, why they are counted this way or that they cannot be linked, and it repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), sections 2.6 and 5.2.2, and Table 8 priority requirements case level data
variable_description: The case-level number of unidentified clients, carried onto the session row as the ceiling that session attendance sits under. The Protocols explain the split: case-level numbers "estimate the total number of unidentified clients who are anticipated to attend services", the session-level number "records how many unidentified clients actually attended that instance of service", and this "prevents double counting". Their worked example is a case with two sessions of 100 unidentified clients each, which means up to 100 distinct people, not 200. Reading it beside UNIDENTIFIEDCLIENTATTENDANCE on the same row is how the two are meant to be used.
description_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), sections 2.6 and 5.2.2, and Table 8 priority requirements case level data
value_definition: A count of people attached to the case rather than to the session, entered as a number up to 999, and repeated on every session record belonging to that case.
limitation: It is an expected ceiling rather than a measured headcount, so it cannot be used as a number of clients served, and adding it up across the sessions of a case counts the same group over and over. It also gives no way to tell how many of the unidentified people at different sessions of a case were the same people, so the true number of distinct attendees lies somewhere between the largest single session and this cap.
rationale: The Protocols set out the case and session split for unidentified clients, state that the case figure is an anticipated total, and give the rule that session attendance must be less than or equal to it.
evidence_quote: Unidentified client numbers captured at the case level estimate the total number of unidentified clients who are anticipated to attend services.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only that it was the total number of unidentified clients across sessions in a case, which reads as a headcount rather than a cap, and it repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

It also does not say what changed, so a corrected spelling and a genuine change to a program's end date look identical, and a record never amended keeps a stale value that is easily mistaken for evidence of currency.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution EDU_APPR_TRN_EXT (PLIDA), column apt_start_date
variable_description: The day the apprenticeship or traineeship on this row began, given by DSS as the "Start date of an apprentice or traineeship event". Only training that touched a Centrelink payment is here, because the table exists to support student and youth payment assessment, so this is not a start date for apprentices in general and cannot be read as a national commencements series. PERIOD_START_DATE sitting beside it is the reporting period the record was extracted in, not the training start, and TYPE_CODE gives the field of education.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution EDU_APPR_TRN_EXT (PLIDA), column apt_start_date
value_definition: A calendar date in YYYY-MM-DD form. The domain is open and there is no code list.
limitation: The date belongs to a training event, not to a person's whole apprenticeship. An apprentice who changes employer part-way through generates a fresh event with a new start date, so counting start dates overstates how many apprenticeships were begun, and EUEA_ID has to be used to collapse the events into episodes.
rationale: The registry's PLIDA distribution of the apprenticeship table defines each column and shows the episode identifier and the reporting period columns that qualify this date.
evidence_quote: Start date of an apprentice or traineeship event.
supersedes_rationale: The entry restated the variable name as 'Apprenticeship start date' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution EDU_APPR_TRN_EXT (PLIDA), column apt_stdnt_end_date
variable_description: The date the apprenticeship or traineeship was expected to finish, which DSS gives as the "Expected end date of an apprentice or traineeship". It is the planned end rather than the observed one, and APT_END_DATE holds the day the event actually stopped. The gap between the two is the usable signal in this table, because a training contract that ends well short of its expected end is the mark of a non-completion, and Centrelink uses the expected end to decide how long a student payment can continue.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution EDU_APPR_TRN_EXT (PLIDA), column apt_stdnt_end_date
value_definition: A calendar date in YYYY-MM-DD form, set when the apprenticeship is registered and revised when the contract changes.
limitation: An expected end date is a plan, not a course length. Because it is revised over the life of a contract, the value in the extract does not reliably measure nominal duration, and it says nothing at all about whether the qualification was awarded.
rationale: The registry defines this column as the expected end date and defines apt_end_date separately as the end of the event, which is the distinction the fplida description was missing.
evidence_quote: Expected end date of an apprentice or traineeship.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Apprenticeship student end date', which reads as a date for the student rather than a planned end, and it repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_domain: ABS Address Register identifier (hashed and truncated)
value_source: ABS Address Register Information Guide
variable_description: The address derived for an income support recipient, for one period bounded by START_DATE and END_DATE. Centrelink holds several addresses for a customer at once, so ADDR_PRTY ranks them and ADR_TYP separates a residence from a postal address; the identifier is the derived winner rather than a raw field. CMTY_CODE marks a discrete community address and CNTRY_CDE carries the country where the address is overseas.
description_source: ABS Address Register Information Guide
value_definition: A hash of the address register identifier, truncated. The ABS Address Register is the ABS's list of every known physical address in Australia, built from Geoscape's Geocoded National Address File and extended with each address's use and its dwelling structure. Hashing replaces the identifier with a code carrying none of the address, so the value has no internal structure and cannot be decoded. There is no finite list to publish.
limitation: The identifier stands for an address, not for a person or a household, so a shared value shows co-residence rather than a relationship. Income support obliges recipients to keep an address current, which makes this source more responsive to a move than most, but a nominee or care arrangement can put a recipient's address somewhere they do not live. Truncating the hash also admits rare collisions, so a shared value is strong evidence of a shared address rather than proof of one.
rationale: The PLIDA DIL gives the field as a hashed, truncated ARID on the DOMINO derived location table, which carries an address priority, an address type and start and end dates. ABS publishes what the Address Register identifier is.
evidence_quote: an up-to-date, comprehensive list of all known physical addresses within Australia
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'not specified' as its domain and the same generic sentence as both its value definition and its limitation.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution MCD_DTLS_EXT (PLIDA), column assmt_id
variable_description: The medical assessment a recorded condition came from, described by DSS as "An assessment ID that links a medical condition to medical assessments". It is the key that ties the primary and secondary condition codes, the impairment rating and the work capacity hours on this row back to one assessment event. Because a person can hold several assessments over the years, each with its own value here, this column is what attributes a change in IMPRMT_RATE or CURR_CAPCTY_NUM to a reassessment rather than to a data correction.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution MCD_DTLS_EXT (PLIDA), column assmt_id
value_definition: An opaque identifier with no published structure and no code list. Values are useful only for grouping rows that belong to one assessment.
limitation: It does not identify the assessor, the type of assessment, or whether the assessment supported a Disability Support Pension claim or an employment services referral; RFRL_RSN_CODE is what records why the assessment was sought. It also carries no date, so IMPRMT_VER_DATE has to be used to place the assessment in time.
rationale: The registry's PLIDA distribution of the medical conditions table defines assmt_id verbatim and lists the impairment, capacity and referral columns that share the assessment it identifies.
evidence_quote: An assessment ID that links a medical condition to medical assessments.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Assessment id' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing on the page explained what the identifier groups or why the same person holds several values.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution INC_EMP_CONT_EXT (PLIDA), column avg_ind
variable_description: Whether the employment income on this row was averaged rather than reported for the days it was actually earned. DSS gives the column as a "Flag indicating employment income was derived by averaging". Centrelink averages earnings where a recipient's pay is irregular or reported over a longer interval, so a flagged row spreads one reported amount evenly across the period instead of recording day-by-day earnings. It qualifies EMP_DLY_INC_CONT and EMP_INC_CONT on the same row, and FREQ_CODE says how often the income was reported.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution INC_EMP_CONT_EXT (PLIDA), column avg_ind
value_definition: A short indicator separating averaged income from income reported as earned. The PLIDA distribution does not publish the code values.
limitation: It says the amount was smoothed but not by how much or over what window. A flagged row therefore cannot date when earnings actually occurred, so an analysis of week-to-week earnings volatility has to set these rows aside rather than treat them as observations of the underlying pay.
rationale: The registry publishes the PLIDA distribution of the continuous employment income table, defining avg_ind and the daily, stated and hours columns it qualifies.
evidence_quote: Flag indicating employment income was derived by averaging.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Income averaged indicator' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, which told a reader nothing about what averaging does to the amounts beside it.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution SNAP_DOMINO_BETA_EXT (PLIDA), column birth_ctry_code
variable_description: The recipient's country of birth as Centrelink holds it, defined by DSS as "The country in which the person was born, as represented by a code". It is a static attribute of the person, carried unchanged on every snapshot row rather than observed at any event. Beside it on the Snap-DOMINO row sit LANG_CODE, the preferred spoken language, and INDIGENOUS, the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status flag; static_demogs adds INTERPRETER_IND, whether an interpreter is needed.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution SNAP_DOMINO_BETA_EXT (PLIDA), column birth_ctry_code
value_definition: A two-character alphabetic code, format AA on the Snap-DOMINO distribution. It is a short DSS code set, not the four-digit ABS Standard Australian Classification of Countries used in Census and survey products; the registry lists a SACC-coded country of birth element separately for other DSS collections.
limitation: Country of birth is not visa status, year of arrival or citizenship, and DOMINO carries none of those, so this column cannot separate a recent arrival from someone who migrated as a child. It is recorded at claim time from what the person stated, and is empty for recipients who were never asked.
rationale: The registry gives the definition and the two-character format on the PLIDA distribution, and lists a distinct SACC 2016 country of birth data element for the Data Exchange, which shows the two collections do not share one classification.
evidence_quote: The country in which the person was born, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Recipient country of birth code' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and gave no hint that the codes are not the ABS classification a user would reach for.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution INC_BUS_EXT (PLIDA), column bus_dly_ass_non_prmy_prdct
variable_description: Daily income Centrelink attributed to the recipient's business assets outside primary production, defined by DSS as "Daily income from non-primary production business assets". It is one of five streams the business income table splits out on a single row: earned, unearned, real estate, primary production assets and non-primary production assets. The split exists because the income test treats these differently, and PERIOD_START_DATE to PERIOD_END_DATE gives the span the daily rate applies over.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution INC_BUS_EXT (PLIDA), column bus_dly_ass_non_prmy_prdct
value_definition: An Australian dollar amount expressed as a rate per day, not a fortnightly or annual total. It is the amount assessed under the social security income test, so it is already net of the deductions those rules allow.
limitation: This is not accounting profit and will not reconcile to what the business reported to the ATO, because Centrelink assesses business income under its own rules and on its own timing. A nil value means nothing was assessed for the period rather than that the assets earned nothing.
rationale: The registry's PLIDA distribution of the business income table defines each of the five income columns verbatim and shows they sit on one row bounded by a reporting period.
evidence_quote: Daily income from non-primary production business assets.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Business daily income from non-primary product assets' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not say that the amount is a daily assessed rate rather than a reported figure.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution INC_BUS_EXT (PLIDA), column bus_dly_ass_prmy_prdct
variable_description: Daily income Centrelink attributed to the recipient's primary production business assets, which DSS defines as "Daily income from primary production business assets" and which covers farming, fishing and forestry. It is kept apart from the non-primary production figure because primary producers are subject to their own averaging and drought concessions in the income test, so the two should not be merged without thought. The amount applies across the period bounded by PERIOD_START_DATE and PERIOD_END_DATE.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution INC_BUS_EXT (PLIDA), column bus_dly_ass_prmy_prdct
value_definition: An Australian dollar amount expressed as a rate per day over the reporting period, assessed under the social security income test rather than reported as accounting income.
limitation: It does not identify the business, the commodity or the holding, and no ABN appears on this table, so a farm here cannot be matched to its BLADE or tax records. A zero cannot be read as a failed season either, since assessment can be deferred or suspended while circumstances are reviewed.
rationale: The registry's PLIDA distribution defines this column and its non-primary production counterpart, and lists every column on the table, which shows no business identifier is carried.
evidence_quote: Daily income from primary production business assets.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Business daily income from primary product assets' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying what primary production means here or why it is separated out.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution INC_BUS_EXT (PLIDA), column bus_dly_inc_earn
variable_description: The part of a recipient's business income that Centrelink treated as earned, given by DSS as "Daily income earned from business activities/assets". The earned and unearned split drives the income test, because earned income attracts concessions such as the working credit and the income free area that unearned income does not, so the two columns record a rules distinction rather than an accounting one. BUS_DLY_INC_UNEARN on the same row carries the other side of the split.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution INC_BUS_EXT (PLIDA), column bus_dly_inc_earn
value_definition: An Australian dollar amount expressed as a rate per day across the reporting period, as assessed under the income test.
limitation: Earned business income is not wages and cannot be turned into an hourly rate: this table has no hours column, unlike inc_emp_cont, which carries EMP_INC_CONT_HRS. A self-employed recipient's labour input is therefore invisible here.
rationale: The registry's PLIDA distribution defines the earned and unearned business income columns and lists the full column set, which shows no hours field on this table.
evidence_quote: Daily income earned from business activities/assets.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Business daily income earned' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so the earned and unearned pair looked like two unexplained amounts rather than an income test distinction.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution INC_BUS_EXT (PLIDA), column bus_dly_inc_real_estate
variable_description: Daily income Centrelink attributed to the recipient's real estate business assets, defined by DSS as "Daily income from real estate business assets" and most often rent from property held in a business structure. BUS_DLY_INC_REAL_ESTATE_CODE beside it records the "Source of real estate income evaluation", which is what separates a valuation from a self-assessment. Both apply across the period bounded by PERIOD_START_DATE and PERIOD_END_DATE.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution INC_BUS_EXT (PLIDA), column bus_dly_inc_real_estate
value_definition: An Australian dollar amount expressed as a rate per day, assessed under the income test rather than taken from a rental statement.
limitation: It counts income, not property. No address, property count or valuation appears, so this column cannot identify landlords or be matched to the ATO rental property schedule, where the ARID does identify the dwelling. Rental income held outside a business structure is assessed elsewhere and does not appear here.
rationale: The registry's PLIDA distribution defines the real estate income column and its companion evaluation source code, and lists every column on the table.
evidence_quote: Daily income from real estate business assets.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Business daily income from real estate' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not mention the evaluation source code that qualifies the amount.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution SNAP_DOMINO_BETA_EXT (PLIDA), column card_any_health_care
variable_description: Whether the person held any kind of Health Care Card on the snapshot date. DSS names the four types it rolls up: the automatic issue card, the ex-Carer Allowance card, the foster child card and the low income card, which are the same four carried individually as CARD_HEALTH_CARE_AUTO, _ECH, _FST and _LOW_INC. It is true when any of those is true and excludes the Pensioner Concession Card and the Commonwealth Seniors Health Card, which have their own flags and their own broader concessions.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution SNAP_DOMINO_BETA_EXT (PLIDA), column card_any_health_care
value_definition: A boolean flag evaluated at SNAP_DATE rather than over a period, so it describes a single day of the year.
limitation: It cannot tell you which card was held, for how long, or whether the card was still pending rather than active. A person who held a card for one day of the year is indistinguishable from one who held a card all year, because the flag is read on the snapshot day alone.
rationale: The registry's Snap-DOMINO PLIDA distribution defines the column as a boolean and lists the four health care card types it covers, and it carries the four individual card flags as separate columns.
evidence_quote: Indicates that the card holder with any of these health care cards
supersedes_rationale: The entry pasted the custodian's run-on wording, which lists the four card types without punctuation, and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 458 'Card: Concession Card, Number of Listed Children'
variable_description: The largest number of children listed on any one of the person's concession cards on the snapshot date. DSS defines it as "The maximum number of children listed on a concession card held by the card holder", so for a person holding several cards it reports the biggest single child list rather than the total across cards. It is the Snap-DOMINO counterpart of EXT_DOM_CHILD_ID_LIST_COUNT on the concession card detail tables, where the individual children are identified.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 458 'Card: Concession Card, Number of Listed Children'
value_definition: A whole number, format {NNNN}N with a maximum of five characters, and 0 supplied as the default where no children are listed.
limitation: Children listed on a card are not children in the household and not dependants for payment purposes. A child can be listed on both parents' cards and so counted twice across the file, while a dependent young person above the listing age is left out entirely, so this is not a count of the person's children.
rationale: The registry's data element gives the definition, the format and the default value, and the Snap-DOMINO PLIDA distribution binds the column to it.
evidence_quote: The maximum number of children listed on a concession card held by the card holder
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'The total number of children listed on a concession card.', which is wrong in the way that matters: the value is a maximum across cards, not a total, and the generic no-value-list sentence stood as both definition and limitation.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 108787 'Card: Concession Card Count'
variable_description: How many concession cards the person held on the snapshot date, across all types. DSS defines it as the "total count of concession cards held by the card holder", so someone holding both a Pensioner Concession Card and a Health Care Card counts two. CARD_ANY is the yes-or-no version of the same fact, and the individual CARD_PENSION and CARD_HEALTH_CARE_* flags say which types make up the count.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, data element 108787 'Card: Concession Card Count'
value_definition: An integer, format N(8), with 0 as the default where no card is held.
limitation: It counts cards, not concessions or their value. A second card usually adds little, because the Pensioner Concession Card already carries the wider set of Commonwealth concessions, so a count of two does not mean twice the benefit. Only cards current on SNAP_DATE are counted, so a card that lapsed the week before is invisible.
rationale: The registry's data element gives the definition, the integer format and the zero default, and the Snap-DOMINO PLIDA distribution binds the column to it.
evidence_quote: indicates the total count of concession cards held by the card holder
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's wording and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence as both value definition and limitation, so nothing said the count is taken on a single snapshot day.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution CCD_HCC_EXT (PLIDA), column card_end_date
variable_description: The day the concession card on this row expires, which DSS states as "The date on which a concession card expires, expressed as YYYY-MM-DD". It is the end of the card's usable life rather than the end of the entitlement behind it: END_REASON_CODE says why the card stopped and PERIOD_END_DATE bounds the reporting period the row was extracted in. With CARD_START_DATE it gives the span over which the card could be presented for a concession.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution CCD_HCC_EXT (PLIDA), column card_end_date
value_definition: A calendar date in YYYY-MM-DD form. Cards are issued for a fixed term, so the value usually sits a set interval after CARD_START_DATE rather than being driven by the recipient's circumstances.
limitation: Expiry is not loss of eligibility. Cards are reissued automatically while entitlement continues, so a person with unbroken eligibility shows a run of consecutive card rows with expiry dates in the middle of it, and treating each expiry as an exit from concession coverage manufactures churn that never happened.
rationale: The registry's PLIDA distribution of the health care card table defines the column as the card's expiry and carries a separate end reason code, which shows expiry and cessation are recorded distinctly.
evidence_quote: The date on which a concession card expires, expressed as YYYY-MM-DD.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Concession card end date' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and left the reader to assume the date marks the end of eligibility rather than the end of a card term.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution SNAP_DOMINO_BETA_EXT (PLIDA), column card_health_care_auto
variable_description: Whether the person held an automatically issued Health Care Card on the snapshot date. DSS notes these cards "are automatically issued to recipients of certain payments", so the card follows the payment rather than being claimed, and the flag sits close to being a marker of JobSeeker, Parenting Payment or a similar allowance. CARD_HEALTH_CARE_LOW_INC covers the separately claimed low income card, and CARD_PENSION the pensioner card that some payments attract instead.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, distribution SNAP_DOMINO_BETA_EXT (PLIDA), column card_health_care_auto
value_definition: A boolean flag evaluated at SNAP_DATE, one value per person per snapshot row.
limitation: It does not name the payment that triggered the card; ISP_TYPE_CODE on the same row is what does that. Nor can it stand in for payment receipt, because several payments carry a Pensioner Concession Card rather than a Health Care Card, and those recipients show false here while still being on income support.
rationale: The registry's Snap-DOMINO PLIDA distribution defines this column as a boolean and states that the card is issued automatically with certain payments, and the same distribution carries the income support payment type code.
evidence_quote: They are automatically issued to recipients of certain payments.
supersedes_rationale: The entry pasted the custodian's two-sentence gloss on Health Care Cards in general and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying that this particular flag is the automatic card only.
